title: Dynamic typing and type()

glossary.definition: The phase when code is converted into a format the computer can run, before the program actually starts executing. Languages like Java check variable types at compile time, but Python checks them later, at runtime. Example: `javac MyProgram.java`
A behind-the-scenes record that keeps track of the active functions your program is currently running. Example: `traceback.print_stack()`

overview.what:
Dynamic typing means variable names are bound to objects at runtime, rather than being locked to a specific data type at compile time. Think of variables as sticky notes with names written on them that can be peeled off an `int` and slapped onto a `str`. The `type()` function acts as a barcode scanner that reveals the actual object's underlying nature.

  user_id = 42
  print(type(user_id))  # <class 'int'>
  user_id = "admin"
  print(type(user_id))  # <class 'str'>

A sharp edge arises when mixing dynamic reassignment with mutable objects. Reassigning a variable moves its reference to a completely new object, but calling methods on the object mutates it in place for all references.

  x = [1, 2]
  y = x
  x = "new type"  # Reassignment: y is unaffected
  x = y
  x.append(3)     # Mutation: y becomes [1, 2, 3]

Because the underlying type dictates whether an object can be mutated in place, this trap is covered fully in `mutable-vs-immutable`.
overview.why: It enables rapid prototyping and highly flexible code since you do not need to declare types upfront. However, this flexibility requires discipline, as a variable unexpectedly pointing to a different type can crash your application deep in the call stack.

why_learning_this: Debugging type errors in JSON payloads where an API expects an `int` but receives a numeric `str`
Writing type-safe Pydantic models by understanding how Python's runtime handles dynamic reassignment

common_mistakes.title: Assuming variables have types
common_mistakes.explanation: Developers from strictly typed languages often think the variable itself holds the type, leading to confusion when `user_id = 123` later becomes `user_id = '123_abc'`. Fix: Remember that types live on the object in memory, not on the variable name.

common_mistakes.title: Misusing type() for inheritance checks
common_mistakes.explanation: Checking types with `type(obj) == dict` fails if the object is a subclass of `dict`, like an `OrderedDict`. Fix: Use `isinstance(obj, dict)` instead when validating object types to safely account for inheritance.

practice_tasks.title: Runtime Type Logger
practice_tasks.prompt: Modify the `log_payload_type(payload)` function so it returns a formatted string like `'Processed payload <value> of type <type_name>'`. Use `type(payload).__name__` to get the type's name.

code_walkthrough.code:
api_response = 404
print('Value:', api_response, '| type:', type(api_response).__name__)

api_response = {'error': 'Not Found'}
print('Value:', api_response, '| type:', type(api_response).__name__)
code_walkthrough.focus: Same name, different type: `api_response` goes from `int` to `dict`, and `type().__name__` follows the object, not the name.

challenge.title: API Response Normalizer
challenge.prompt: Build a webhook receiver helper `normalize_webhook_data(data)` that inspects the dynamic type of `data`. If it is a `str`, return it converted to `int` (assume a valid numeric string). If it is already an `int`, return it as-is. If it is a `float`, return it cast to `int`. Otherwise return `0`. Use `isinstance()` here to practice safe runtime type checking.

recall_questions.q: What built-in function reveals the underlying type of an object in Python?
recall_questions.answer: The `type()` function. For example, `type(42)` returns `<class 'int'>` and `type('hi')` returns `<class 'str'>`.

recall_questions.q: In Python, are types bound to the variable name or the object itself?
recall_questions.answer: Types are bound to the object itself, not the variable name. So when you write `x = 42` and then `x = 'hello'`, the variable `x` just points to a new object — the integer `42` still exists as an `int` in memory.

understanding_checks.question: What will be printed when this code is executed?
understanding_checks.why: In Python, types are bound to the object, not the variable name. The variable `x` is simply reassigned to a string object, so `type()` returns the string type.

understanding_checks.question: A developer claims that `x = 10` permanently restricts `x` to holding integers. Why is this incorrect in Python?
understanding_checks.answer: Variables are merely references to objects in memory. They do not have fixed types.
understanding_checks.why: This is the essence of dynamic typing: the type information lives on the object, not on the variable name.

understanding_checks.question: What will be printed when this code is executed?
understanding_checks.code:
items = [1, 2]
backup = items
items.append(3)
items = "empty"
print(backup)
understanding_checks.why: Calling `items.append(3)` mutates the shared `list` object, so `backup` sees the change. Reassigning `items = "empty"` points the `items` label to a new `str` object, but leaves `backup` pointing to the mutated `list`.
